line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 b6 c3 Qd7
teaches: A plan to trade off your worst piece can fail on a single check — before playing the trade, look at the square the enemy queen would check from once the recapture lands. One quiet preparing move is the difference between a good plan and a lost piece.
explains: The plan is to trade off the bad light-squared bishop, and the reflex is just to do it now — but look one move further first. Trade immediately and it opens a check, with the queen landing to fork your king and the piece that recaptured. So the queen steps to d7 first: it covers the a4 check-square and keeps the bishop on c8 defended for its coming trip. One quiet move, and the fork never exists.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 b6 c3 Qd7 Bd3 Ba6 Ne2
teaches: Where a knight goes should be decided by which PAWN you mean to advance later — the natural central square sits in front of the f-pawn and quietly cancels its charge, while the square beside it does the same defensive work and leaves the pawn free.
explains: Where should the knight go? Let the pawn you want to push decide. The natural square in front of the f-pawn would quietly kill the plan of ever running it — so the knight comes to e2 instead. It still holds d4 and c3 and covers f4, but now the f-pawn is unobstructed behind it. Castle, then let that pawn charge at the base of the enemy chain.
